study_identification_part.si4_title: Dynamic gray matter volume changes in pediatric multiple sclerosis: A 3.5 year MRI study

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To assess the spatial patterns of gray matter atrophy in pediatric patients with multiple sclerosis, their dynamic changes over time, and their clinical relevance using MRI.

rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.answer: SPM12; Longitudinal registration; DARTEL (diffeomorphic anatomical registration using exponentiated lie algebra); Segmentation; MNI normalization; 4-mm Gaussian smoothing; Lesion refilling

Lesion refilling was also performed before GM volumetric analysis.
rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.supporting_text: Regional GM growth modeling in HC and the evaluation of deviations from normative data in patients with MS required the alignment of participant images to Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) standard space. Taking into account the longitudinal consistency of MRI scans belonging to the same participant, within-subject serial longitudinal registration as implemented in SPM 12 was used to align the available 3D T1-weighted images (either 2 or 3). [...] Then, GM and WM segmented images of all participants, in the closest possible rigid-body alignment with each other, were used to produce initial GM and WM templates and to drive the deformation to the templates. At each iteration, the deformations, calculated using the diffeomorphic anatomical registration using exponentiated lie algebra (DARTEL) registration method, were applied to GM and WM, with an increasingly good alignment of participant morphology, to produce templates. clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Linear models (SPM12) were used to estimate mean z scores across all MS patients and their correlations with clinical and lesional variables (disease duration, EDSS, premorbid IQ full scale and subscales, T2 LV, T1 LV) at baseline. For longitudinal data in the follow-up cohort (n=30), linear models adjusted for follow-up duration, baseline EDSS, and disease duration were applied to estimate z score changes over time and their correlations with baseline IQ and lesion volume changes. Between-group comparisons used Pearson χ2 test, Mann-Whitney U test, 2-sample t test, and linear mixed effects models. Results were tested at p<0.05 family-wise error corrected, with exploratory analyses at p<0.001 uncorrected (cluster extent=50 voxels). Key findings: Higher EDSS correlated with more severe GM damage in bilateral thalamus, left caudate, left inferior frontal gyrus, and right precuneus; longer disease duration correlated with more severe GM damage in cingulate, frontal, and temporal regions; higher IQ scores correlated with less severe GM damage in multiple regions; higher T2/T1 LV correlated with more severe GM damage in thalamus, caudate, frontal and temporal lobes. For longitudinal changes: higher baseline IQ correlated with lower GM loss progression in cingulate, frontal, parietal, occipital, and temporal regions; T2/T1 LV changes correlated with GM atrophy progression in bilateral thalamus, postcentral gyrus, and left precentral gyrus.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Pediatric MS patients showed failures in GM development in multiple cortical and subcortical regions, with continued GM atrophy progression over 3.5 years that was only partially related to focal WM lesions, suggesting early neurodegenerative phenomena; higher IQ was associated with reduced GM deviations and slower atrophy progression.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: At baseline, pediatric MS patients (n=68) exhibited significant negative deviations from sex- and age-expected GM volumes in numerous regions including basal ganglia (thalamus, caudate), hippocampus, and cortical areas in frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes, and cerebellum (p<0.05 FWE-corrected; mean z-scores ranging from -0.55 to -1.41). No regions showed positive deviations. During 3.5-year follow-up (n=30), most regions showed progressive worsening of deviations (especially bilateral thalamus, putamen, supplementary motor area, cingulate cortex, precentral/postcentral gyri), while a few regions (left inferior parietal lobule, superior parietal lobule, supramarginal gyrus, angular gyrus, middle temporal gyrus) showed reduced deviations over time (p<0.001 uncorrected). Higher EDSS correlated with more severe GM damage in thalamus (r=-0.42 to -0.38), caudate (r=-0.45), and frontal regions. Higher premorbid IQ (total, verbal, performance subscales) correlated with less GM damage at baseline (r=0.45-0.62) and slower atrophy progression during follow-up (r=0.43-0.71) in cingulate cortex, thalamus, and frontal, temporal, parietal, and cerebellar regions. Focal WM lesion volumes (T2 and T1 LV) correlated with GM damage in thalamus (r=-0.54 to -0.59), caudate, and frontal/temporal regions, but many regions with GM deviations showed no correlation with WM lesions, suggesting primary GM involvement independent of WM inflammation.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Small longitudinal cohort (n=30); only IQ assessed as reserve measure (other factors like socioeconomic status and leisure activities not collected); clinical stability during follow-up prevented analysis of disability worsening prediction; relatively short follow-up duration
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: This study is not without limitations. First, only part of our patients underwent a clinical and MRI follow-up assessment. Although the number of patients assessed at follow-up may seem small (n = 30), it should be considered that the prevalence of pediatric MS is relatively low. Second, we analyzed only IQ as a possible measure of reserve. Other factors, such as socioeconomic characteristics and leisure activities, which have not been collected in our patients, should be included in future analyses. Finally, the clinical stability of our patients during the study period did not allow any analysis of prediction of disability worsening. As a consequence, a longer follow-up is needed to ascertain the clinical relevance of GM volumetric abnormalities in pediatric patients with MS.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study used heterochromic maturational analysis to examine region-specific developmental trajectories, revealing that different GM regions follow distinct maturational timelines. First-order derivatives of the normative model were evaluated at each age decile to test for nullity of growth rate and identify maturational peaks. The inverted U-shape developmental trajectory was confirmed across regions, with higher-order association areas maturing after lower-order sensorimotor regions. Sex-stratified trajectories showed divergence starting around puberty (12.1 years), with males showing more prolonged positive growth in frontal/temporal regions and basal ganglia compared to females. The study distinguished two mechanisms of GM damage: (1) inflammation-dependent damage related to WM lesions affecting highly connected regions (thalamus, caudate) early in disease, and (2) primary GM involvement independent of WM lesions. Some regions showed reduced deviations over time, potentially reflecting plateauing of tissue loss or reparative mechanisms (plasticity, remyelination) in young patients. Lesion refilling was performed before GM volumetric analysis to prevent bias from focal WM lesions. Intracranial volume was not used for normalization because brain-skull growth dissociates in pediatric MS.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This study used a large external reference cohort (NIH-funded MRI Study of Normal Brain Development, n=317) to overcome the difficulty of obtaining longitudinal MRI scans from pediatric healthy controls. The NIH HC data were acquired at 6 pediatric centers on 1.5T scanners (GE and Siemens), while the local HSR HC (n=26) and MS patients were scanned on a 3.0T Philips scanner. Scanner/protocol differences were addressed by including magnetic field strength as a covariate in the normative model, which was validated to have minimal impact (lowest partial correlation r values) compared to biological effects. The NIH HC dataset included 163 subjects followed once (median 2.0 years) and 154 followed twice (median 3.9 years), spanning ages 4.2-22.3 years. At baseline, all 68 MS patients were receiving disease-modifying treatments (interferon-β n=41, glatiramer acetate n=16, natalizumab n=11), and none changed treatment during follow-up. Sixteen patients (23%) showed low IQ (range 70-90), including 5 with and 11 without follow-up. During follow-up, median EDSS remained stable (p=0.28), with median annualized relapse rate of 0 (range 0-1.23). T2 lesion volumes did not change significantly (p=0.06), but T1 lesion volumes increased significantly (p=0.03). The study population was entirely Caucasian and right-handed. The modeling approach assumed homoscedastic errors, which may not fully capture age- and site-dependent variance heterogeneity.
